title: “COME, MY BELOVED, LET US GO OUT”: The Woman in Scripture Who Openly Expressed Romantic Desire
paragraphs: “COME, MY BELOVED, LET US GO OUT”: The Woman in Scripture Who Openly Expressed Romantic Desire

The Bible did not silence her desire. It preserved her words in Scripture—and what she says may completely change the way you think about love, marriage, intimacy, shame, and the God who created the human heart.
There is a woman in the Bible who says something so intimate, so confident, and so startlingly human that many Christians can read past it without realizing what just happened.
She does not merely wait to be admired.
She speaks.
She desires.
She invites.
And the Holy Spirit allowed her words to remain in Scripture.
Listen to the Hebrew:
אֲנִי לְדוֹדִי וְעָלַי תְּשׁוּקָתוֹ
Ani ledodi, ve'alai teshuqato.
“I am my beloved’s, and his desire is for me.”
Then she continues:
לְכָה דוֹדִי נֵצֵא הַשָּׂדֶה
Lekhah dodi, netze hasadeh.
“Come, my beloved, let us go out into the field.”
And then comes the line many people were never prepared to hear a woman in Scripture say:
שָׁם אֶתֵּן אֶת־דֹּדַי לָךְ
Sham etten et-dodai lakh.
“There I will give my love to you.”
Song of Songs 7:11–13.
Read that again.
Slowly.
Because whatever else we do with this passage, we should not make it less human than God allowed it to be.
This is not pornography.
It is not vulgarity.
It is not a woman being shamed for having affection.
It is biblical poetry celebrating love.
And the woman is not voiceless inside it.
She knows she is desired.
She desires in return.
She speaks openly to the man she loves.
“Come, my beloved…”

There is something almost shocking about that when you have spent years around versions of Christianity that sometimes treated every discussion of romantic desire as though holiness required pretending human beings had no bodies.
Some people were taught to fear desire more than they were taught to understand it.
Some women learned that modesty meant becoming emotionally invisible.
Some men learned that attraction itself was dirty rather than something requiring holiness, wisdom, self-control, and covenant faithfulness.

Some young Christians became terrified by normal feelings because nobody taught them the difference between temptation and sin, between desire and exploitation, between covenant intimacy and lust that consumes another person.
So they hid.
They prayed desperately for God to remove feelings He never said were inherently sinful.
They carried shame into marriage.
And some discovered something painful.
A wedding ceremony can change your marital status overnight.
It cannot automatically heal years of shame.
Then Song of Songs opens its mouth.
And suddenly there is fragrance.
Vineyards.
Pomegranates.
Longing.
Beauty.
Mutual affection.
A woman speaking.
A man responding.
Two people delighting in one another without Scripture apologizing for their humanity.
That matters.
The Hebrew word in Song of Songs 7:11 translated “desire” is תְּשׁוּקָה — teshuqah.
Her beloved’s desire is directed toward her.
Then she answers that desire not with embarrassed silence but with invitation:
“Come, my beloved…”
Notice what the passage does not say.
It does not teach that every desire is holy.
It does not authorize adultery.
It does not erase sexual boundaries.
It does not make lust harmless.
And it certainly does not teach that another human being exists for our consumption.
The wider witness of Scripture refuses all of those conclusions.

Jesus takes sexual sin seriously enough to address lust at the level of the heart (Matthew 5:27–30). Paul commands believers to flee sexual immorality and reminds Christians that their bodies belong to God (1 Corinthians 6:18–20). Hebrews tells believers to honor marriage and keep the marriage bed undefiled (Hebrews 13:4).
Christian holiness is not permission to use another person.
But neither is holiness hatred of the body.
That distinction is enormous.
Because the God who says “flee sexual immorality” is also the God whose Scriptures contain the Song of Songs.
Maybe some of us have spent so much time running from what sexuality can become when corrupted that we have forgotten who created human beings in the first place.
Before there was pornography, there was Eden.
Before there was adultery, there was covenant.
Before there was sexual exploitation, there was the declaration:
“male and female he created them.”
Genesis 1:27.
And after creating humanity embodied as male and female, God looked upon what He had made and called His creation “very good” (Genesis 1:31).
Sin did not invent the human body.
God did.
Sin corrupts.
God creates.
That difference changes everything.
Song of Songs does not invite us to worship desire.
It teaches us that desire does not have to become a god in order to be acknowledged as human.
And perhaps that is where this becomes painfully personal.
Because maybe your story with desire is not beautiful.
Maybe yours became secret.
Maybe somebody used you.
Maybe you used somebody.
Maybe pornography rewired the way you learned to look at people.
Maybe an affair destroyed trust.
Maybe you crossed boundaries you once swore you never would.
Maybe you gave your body hoping somebody would finally give you love.
Maybe you confused being wanted with being valued.
Maybe you stayed in a relationship because loneliness frightened you more than compromise.
Maybe you have been married for years, yet shame still follows you into the bedroom.
Maybe nobody violated you.
Nobody abandoned you.
Nothing dramatic happened.
You simply learned somewhere along the way that being deeply human made God disappointed in you.
And so you became very good at hiding.
Church clothes.
Bible open.
Worship music playing.
Hands raised.
Search history deleted.
Messages erased.
Memories buried.
Questions unanswered.
Smiling when someone asks how you are doing.
But God sees the whole person standing behind the Christian vocabulary.
And this is where Song of Songs cannot save you.
Romance cannot save you.
Marriage cannot save you.
Sex cannot save you.
Being desired cannot save you.
Being married to the person of your dreams cannot save you.
There is a deeper hunger underneath every human hunger.
And eventually every created thing collapses beneath the weight of being asked to become a Savior.
That is where Jesus Christ enters the story.
Not as the destroyer of humanity.
As its Redeemer.
The Christian Gospel is not the announcement that respectable people have finally learned to suppress themselves well enough for God to tolerate them.
The Gospel is the announcement that sinners who could never cleanse themselves have been offered reconciliation with God through Jesus Christ.
Christ came into our scandal.
Our lust.
Our pride.
Our adultery.
Our secret fantasies.
Our broken marriages.
Our loneliness.
Our self-righteousness.
Our wounds.
Our shame.
Our attempts to find in another body what only God can ultimately give.
And He did something scandalous with scandal.
He carried sin to a cross.
“For our sake he made him to be sin who knew no sin, so that in him we might become the righteousness of God.”
2 Corinthians 5:21.
That is Christianity.
Not pretending you never sinned.
Not renaming sin so repentance becomes unnecessary.
Not drowning in shame as though Christ's blood were insufficient.
Repentance and grace meet at the cross.
Jesus does not say sin does not matter.
The cross proves precisely how much it matters.
But the cross also declares that your sin does not have to write the final sentence of your life.
Maybe that is what somebody reading this needed tonight.
Your worst chapter does not have to become your title.
The affair does not have to become your identity.
The addiction does not have to become your name.
The abuse committed against you does not determine your worth.
The thing you did does not become righteous merely because God loves you—but neither is the repentant sinner beyond the reach of Christ because the thing was terrible.
There is forgiveness.
There is cleansing.
There is transformation.
There is a new way to live.
“There is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus.”
Romans 8:1.
Do not turn that verse into permission to remain chained.
It is an invitation to come out of the prison.
Grace does not merely whisper, “You are forgiven.”
Grace begins teaching the forgiven person how to walk free.

And suddenly the woman saying, “Come, my beloved,” can teach us something deeper—not because Song of Songs should be flattened into an allegory in which every romantic sentence secretly means Jesus, but because its celebration of rightly ordered human love reminds us that redemption does not make us less human.
Christ restores us toward what holiness was always meant to be.
Not numbness.
Not shame.
Not exploitation.
Not uncontrolled appetite.
Wholeness.
A heart learning to love without possessing.
Eyes learning to see people rather than objects.
A body surrendered to God rather than ruled by appetite.
A marriage where tenderness does not need to apologize.
A single life where holiness does not mean worthlessness.
A wounded life where healing is possible.
A fallen life where repentance can become the doorway to restoration.
And there is another beautiful detail in the woman's words.
She says:
אֲנִי לְדוֹדִי
Ani ledodi.
“I am my beloved’s.”
There is belonging here.
Not consumption.
Not anonymous bodies.
Not scrolling.
Not swiping through human beings as though souls were products.
Belonging.
And that should confront our generation.
We have never had greater technological access to bodies while remaining capable of extraordinary loneliness.
We can see almost anything and know almost nobody.
We can collect attention and still ache to be known.
We can receive hundreds of reactions and wonder whether one person would remain after seeing everything.
Because lust says:
“What can I take from you?”
Love asks:
“How can I seek your good?”
Lust reduces.
Love recognizes.
Lust consumes the image.
Covenant remains when the image changes.
And the Gospel goes deeper still.
Jesus knew what was inside us before we cleaned anything up.
He knew the browser history.
The memory.
The betrayal.
The craving.
The hypocrisy.
The secret.
And He still called sinners to repentance and offered mercy.
That does not make sin small.
It makes grace astonishing.
Somebody reading this has spent years trying to punish themselves for something Jesus is calling them to bring into the light.
You cannot repent of the person you keep pretending does not exist.
Stop hiding.
Bring the truth to Christ.
If necessary, confess to the person you have sinned against and seek wise pastoral or professional help where appropriate.
Install the boundaries.
End the affair.
Delete the secret account.
Stop feeding the fantasy.
Tell someone trustworthy.
Seek reconciliation where reconciliation is safe and appropriate.
And where another person's sin wounded you, hear this carefully:
Their sin does not make you dirty.
You are not required to call evil good in order to forgive.
You are not required to return yourself to an unsafe person to prove you love Jesus.
Healing can be slow.
But Christ is not frightened by wounds.
Look at the risen Jesus.
He conquered death, yet His resurrected body still bore scars.
Scars were not the evidence that death won.
They became witnesses that death had lost.
Maybe yours can become witnesses too.
Not because everything that happened was good.
It wasn't.
But because Jesus Christ can write redemption into places sin intended to destroy.
That is why our heartbeat at Gospel Warrior remains:
Not because every earthly consequence disappears.
Not because repentance magically repairs every relationship.
Not because Christians never struggle again.
But because the Gospel means your story no longer has to end where sin left you.
Be human.
Be honest.
You do not owe strangers the details of your story.
Sometimes those three words are enough.
The married couple silently struggling with intimacy.
The teenager drowning in shame.
The believer secretly battling pornography.
The woman who thinks her past destroyed her worth.
The man who has never told anyone what he is fighting.
The Christian who confused holiness with hating their own humanity.
The person who does not even believe in Jesus yet but desperately needs to discover that Christianity is not about polishing sinners until they look respectable.
It is about a Savior who raises the dead.
Better yet, send this privately when privacy is kinder.
Because shame has a strange way of returning after conviction fades, and you may need these words again:
Desire is not your god.
Shame is not your master.
Sin is not your identity.
Jesus Christ is still calling people out of darkness.
And grace is still stronger than the chapter you wish you could erase.
If Gospel Warrior has been feeding your faith, you can also help this ministry continue.
It doesn't.
It doesn't.
Scripture says that giving should come from a willing heart, “not reluctantly or under compulsion” (2 Corinthians 9:7).
A Facebook share can travel farther than you imagine.
The discount is a thank-you.
It is not the reason to give.
Jesus is not for sale.
Grace is not merchandise.
Support simply helps the work continue.
Follow Jesus.
Open your Bible.
Pray when nobody is watching.
Repent quickly.
Forgive deeply.
Love faithfully.
Fight secret sin.
Protect the vulnerable.
Honor your marriage.
Honor your singleness.
Refuse to turn another human being into an object.
And when you fall, do not build a house in the mud.
Run back to Christ.
Because thousands of years ago, Scripture preserved the voice of a woman who was not ashamed to say:
“Come, my beloved…”
Her desire was not erased from the Bible.
It was written into it.
And perhaps the deeper shock for some of us is not that Scripture can speak honestly about desire.
Perhaps the shock is discovering that God has never needed our pretending.
He wants truth in the inward being.
He wants the hidden person.
The wounded person.
The tempted person.
The ashamed person.
The person behind the Sunday face.
He calls sinners to repentance not so He can humiliate them, but because Christ came to save sinners.
But above everything else—
come to Christ.
Because one day every romance ends at the edge of eternity.
Every beautiful body grows old.
Every human embrace eventually has to loosen.
Every earthly beloved is mortal.
And when everything temporary falls from your hands, only One can carry you through death itself.
His name is Jesus.
The chapter you are most ashamed to let anyone read may become the very page where someone finally sees what the grace of Jesus Christ can do.
